Question_text: A student measures the spring constant k of a spring using two different methods. The spring constant k of a spring is a measure of the stiffness of the spring. The larger the spring constant k, the more difficult the spring is to stretch.

Parts.part_text: Measure the unstretched length lo of the spring to the nearest 0.1 cm. Do not include the loops at the end of the spring in your measurement.
Parts.image: A full-size diagram of a coiled spring, with dashed lines indicating its unstretched length. The spring has multiple coils.

Parts.part_text: The student: attaches the spring to a clamp on a stand; suspends a 300 g mass from the spring. The arrangement of apparatus is shown in Fig. 1.2. The student measures the new length l₁ of the spring. l₁ = 17.6 cm. Calculate the extension e of the spring produced by the mass. Use the equation: e = l₁ - lo.
Parts.image: A diagram showing a spring suspended from a clamp and stand. A 300g mass is attached to the bottom of the spring, stretching it. Labels indicate 'clamp', 'spring', and '300 g mass'.

Parts.part_text: Calculate the spring constant k₁ of the spring. Use the equation: k₁ = 300/e.
It is important to avoid line-of-sight (parallax) errors when determining the extension of the spring. Explain what is meant by parallax errors and how to avoid parallax errors.

The student: pulls the 300 g mass down by a small distance and releases it so that the mass oscillates up and down; measures the time t₁ taken for 20 oscillations. The reading on the stop-watch is shown in Fig. 1.3. Record this time t₁ in Table 1.1 to one decimal place.
Parts.image: A digital stopwatch display showing '00.13.58' with 'min' and 'sec' labels, indicating 13.58 seconds.

Parts.part_text: The student measures the time for 20 oscillations once more and records the time t₂ in Table 1.1. Calculate the mean time t for 20 oscillations and record your answer in Table 1.1.
The mean period T of the oscillation is the mean time taken for one oscillation. Calculate the mean period T. Calculate the value of T². Record all your values in Table 1.1.
Use your value of T² from Table 1.1 to calculate the spring constant k₂ of the spring. Use the equation: k₂ = 11.8/T².
Explain why the value for the mean period T obtained by measuring 20 oscillations twice is more accurate than the value obtained by measuring 1 oscillation twice.

Question_text: A student investigates the rate of cooling of water at the top and at the bottom of a beaker of hot water.

Parts.part_text: The student: measures the room temperature dr as dr = 22.5 °C; pours 200 cm³ of hot water into a beaker; lowers a thermometer into the beaker until its bulb is just covered by the hot water, as shown in Fig. 2.1.
Parts.image: Diagram showing a thermometer suspended by a clamp and stand, with its bulb immersed in water within a beaker. Labels indicate 'thermometer', 'water', and 'stand'.

Parts.part_text: waits for approximately 30 s; starts a stop-watch and reads the thermometer. The temperature on the thermometer at time t = 0 is shown in Fig. 2.2. Record the temperature reading at time t = 0 to the nearest 0.5°C in Table 2.1.
Parts.image: Close-up of a mercury-in-glass thermometer scale marked in degrees Celsius. The mercury level is between 80 °C and 90 °C, indicating 86.0 °C.

Parts.part_text: Explain why the student waits for 30s before reading the initial temperature of the hot water.

The student waits for 3 minutes, reads the thermometer and records the new temperature reading in Table 2.1. The student then: removes the thermometer from the beaker and pours the water away; repeats the procedure in (a), but lowers the thermometer into the beaker, so that the bulb is just above, but not touching the bottom of the beaker, as shown in Fig. 2.3. records the initial and final temperatures of the water as shown in Table 2.1.
Parts.image: Diagram showing a thermometer suspended by a clamp and stand, with its bulb immersed just above the bottom of water within a beaker. Labels indicate 'thermometer', 'water', and 'stand'.

Parts.part_text: Calculate the average rate of cooling P₁ of the hot water at the top of the beaker. Use the equation: average rate of cooling = decrease in temperature of the water / time taken. Give your answer to 2 significant figures and state the unit.
Use the data in Table 2.1 on page 7 to calculate the average rate of cooling P_B of the hot water at the bottom of the beaker.
Use your answers to (b)(i) and (b)(ii) to suggest why a hot liquid should be stirred before measuring its temperature.
State one way in which the apparatus in this experiment is arranged to make it easy to read the thermometer accurately.
The experiment is repeated to check the results. Suggest one variable that must be kept constant.
The student leaves the thermometer in the hot water and waits for 30 minutes before reading the thermometer again. Predict a value for the temperature of the water in the beaker.

Question_text: A student investigates how the potential difference V across the terminals of a power supply changes as the current I in a circuit changes. The student assembles the circuit shown in Fig. 3.1.

Parts.part_text: The student closes the switch and observes the reading Vo on the voltmeter. The reading is shown in Fig. 3.2. Record the voltmeter reading Vo.
Parts.image: A circuit diagram showing a power supply connected in series with an ammeter (A) and a resistance wire. A voltmeter (V) is connected across the power supply terminals. A crocodile clip is connected to one end of the resistance wire (X) and a flying lead. Insulating tape is used along the resistance wire with a scale from 0 to 100 cm. The voltmeter shown in Fig. 3.2 is a circular analog dial with a scale from 0 to 3 V, with the needle pointing to 2.8 V.

Parts.part_text: The student then: connects the crocodile clip to the resistance wire at a distance d = 100.0cm from end X; records the potential difference V across the wire as V = 2.3V; records the current I in the wire; opens the switch.

The reading on the ammeter is shown in Fig. 3.3. Record the ammeter reading I. The student: closes the switch; repeats (b) for values of d = 80.0cm, 60.0cm, 40.0cm and 20.0cm. The student’s results are shown in Table 3.1. Complete the header of each column. Include the value of I from (b).
Parts.image: A circular analog ammeter dial with a scale from 0 to 1 A, marked with 0.5 A. The needle points between 0.5 A and 1 A, at approximately 0.7 A.

Parts.part_text: On the grid provided in Fig. 3.4, plot a graph of V on the y-axis against I on the x-axis, using the data in Table 3.1. Start both axes from the origin (0, 0). Draw the best-fit straight line.
Parts.image: A blank grid with axes labeled V/V (y-axis) and I/A (x-axis) for plotting a graph.

Parts.part_text: The gradient m of your line is numerically equal to the resistance r of the power supply. Calculate the gradient of your line. Show clearly on the graph the values you chose and show your working.
The intercept between the y-axis and your line is the electromotive force V₀ of the power supply. Extend your best-fit line to meet the y-axis and write down the value of V₀.

Compare the value of V₀ in (a) with the value of V₀ you obtained from the graph in (e)(ii). Two quantities can be considered to be equal within the limits of experimental accuracy if their values are within 10% of each other. State whether your results show that the two values obtained for the electromotive force are the same. Support your statement with a calculation.

Another student decides to connect the crocodile clip in Fig. 3.1 so that there is only a very small length of the resistance wire included in the circuit. The teacher tells the student not to do this. Suggest one practical reason why values of d less than 20.0cm should not be used.

It is possible to change the potential difference V by using a variable resistor rather than using different lengths of resistance wire. Complete the circuit diagram in Fig. 3.5 to show how the variable resistor is connected.
Parts.image: An incomplete circuit diagram showing an ammeter (A) and a voltmeter (V) symbol. There is an open switch and two connection points where a variable resistor should be added.

Question_text: A student investigates the average speed of a trolley moving along a horizontal bench. The trolley is placed on a ramp and released from rest. Some of the apparatus used is shown in Fig. 4.1. The stopping distance of the trolley is the distance moved by the trolley from the bottom of the ramp until it comes to rest. Plan an experiment to investigate how the average speed of the trolley along the bench until it comes to rest depends upon its mass. The average speed of the trolley can be calculated using the equation shown: average speed = stopping distance / time. In your plan you should: explain briefly how to carry out the investigation, stating any other apparatus needed; state the key variables to keep constant; draw a table with column headings to show how to display the readings (you are not required to enter any readings into the table); explain how to use your readings to reach a conclusion.
image: A diagram showing a ramp leading down to a horizontal bench. A trolley is positioned on the ramp, and a set of masses are placed on the trolley. A stand supports the ramp. Labels indicate 'stand', 'set of masses', 'trolley', 'ramp', and 'bench'.
